raw_response.publication_year_note: Primary journal volume/article year is 2023 (Environ Monit Assess (2023) 195:138); published online 22 November 2022 with 2022 copyright line.
raw_response.rationale: This cross-sectional household survey in Osun State, Nigeria (548 recruited, N = 542 analytic sample in water-source tables) does not empirically measure or test state/national WASH policy or donor institutional reforms (which are discussed only narratively). However, it explicitly tests residential housing tenure (Owner vs caretaker/tenant and Household owned/occupied vs Tenants only) against household water service access outcomes (SWiM Family A: housing/property tenure). In bivariate cross-tabulations (Table 4, PDF p. 9, N = 542), house owners had significantly higher safely managed (19.3% vs 15.5%) and basic (67.2% vs 58.2%) drinking water service and lower unimproved service (13.5% vs 26.3%) than caretakers/tenants (Pearson chi2 = 13.830, df = 2, P = 0.001; see also residential occupancy category chi2 = 15.843, df = 6, P = 0.015, and domestic water service in Table 5, PDF p. 10, Owner vs caretaker/tenant chi2 = 5.822, P = 0.054). In the multivariable binary logistic regression predicting composite household water security (Table 7, PDF p. 12, adjusting for age, wealth quartiles, water treatment, and toilet type), Household owned/occupied vs Tenants only (Ref) yielded a non-significant adjusted OR = 1.12 (95% CI: 0.62–2.024, p = 0.708; Landlord/tenants occupied OR = 0.975, 95% CI: 0.56–1.699, p = 0.929). Confidence is rated medium because tenure is operationalized as a generic owner-versus-tenant occupancy variable within a sociodemographic predictor battery rather than an analysis of formal land-title or tenancy-law rules.
